utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Registrar, please have the accused brought in, if he's there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to say good morning to the interpreters, who must be ready, I suppose. I think I have to apologise on behalf of this whole Tribunal for this delay, which is due to external reasons, as you all know, and I hope that it was not too disturbing for the witness. Therefore, I think we shall end this hearing at 1.30 as expected, but maybe we could have only one break during the morning, a 20-minute break in an hour, approximately. Is that convenient? Would General Blaskic agree with this? We would sit until 12.30, we would have a 20-minute break, and we would adjourned at 1.30. I would not like to make the hearing longer. We could stop at 1.30 as scheduled. Would that be convenient, General?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you for asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Nobilo, let's resume our proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: General, we left off yesterday with September. We finished September. Would you now tell us about the events of October 1993?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours. On the 1st of October, 1993, I issued an order to the assistant for personnel at the Operative Zone command to prepare documentation for all appointments which were to have been okayed by the Defence Ministry of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. At the beginning of October, we had some problems with the fact that people were leaving the front. Soldiers were leaving the front of their own accord, and the military police went to fetch those soldiers and take them in, those who had left the front line towards the BH army. In the course of the day, I received information from the assistant for security that the protagonists of the unrest in the Lasva pocket were, for the most part, refugees and that the Croat refugees from Zenica presented a particular problem. So these were, in fact, displaced persons, refugees. I informed my associates about the visit of the chief of the main staff, and I informed them of the questions that I had discussed with the chief of the main staff. I emphasised the question of the multiple chains of command and the single responsibility in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone command. I also received more detailed information from the chief of the main staff about the formation of a forward command post of the main staff of the HVO in Kiseljak within Operative Group number 2, its headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just a moment, please, General. Tell the Court, please, what we mean when we say "forward command post of the main staff"? What was its function and who performed this? What did it, in fact, mean for their chain of command?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, the forward command post of the main staff in Kiseljak was directly in command of Operative Group 2 of Kiseljak, Kresevo, and the remaining parts of the municipality of Fojnica and parts of the Vares municipality. Usually, in this forward command post, you would have either the deputy of the chief of the main staff or a high officer of the main staff appointed by the chief of the main staff of the HVO sent there to be on location at the forward command post. In the chain of command, this meant direct command over Operative Group 2 in Kiseljak by the main staff of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The first information that you received, you received at the end of September 1993 with regard to the establishment of a forward command post in Kiseljak. What were you told? For how long was this forward command post to be in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I was told that it had already been in existence for several months, and this was told to me by the chief of the main staff of the HVO. I was told, at the end of September, that this was functioning already for several months, had been functioning for several months. It was already functioning for more than a month; that is certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was this the only forward command post of the main staff at that time or did another exist?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, there was another forward command post in Prozor, but that was the other zone of responsibility. It was the north-west Herzegovina zone, and possibly there were forward command posts in other positions, but I was not aware of them. I don't know whether they existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I received summary information from the command of the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade that, in the course of September 1993, a disciplinary investigation was undertaken against various individuals, that is to say, 60 soldiers in all, and that in the zone of responsibility of the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade, there were about six extraordinary incidents and events. I received information from the Vitez Brigade, for example, that there had been heavy human losses on the front line and that the commander of the brigade did not have the necessary manpower to fill in the units lacking a sufficient number of soldiers. He asked me that recruits be engaged, women for this to fill up the units, so that the men could take over the role -- that is to say, that the men should be sent to the front line in the Vitez area. I was also informed of the fact that the front line was being deserted en masse and that the snipers were constantly shooting from Stari Vitez in the city centre, the centre of Vitez itself, that there was sniper fire. In the afternoon, I visited the recruits in Nova Bila, and I also received information as to the situation in the centre for the training of new recruits, from the commander of the centre for training in Nova Bila. On the 2nd of October, 1993, in the afternoon in Vitez, an incident broke out when a patrol was denied passage, a patrol of the European Monitoring Mission. There were four members of the mission in a vehicle, and what happened was that there was a burst of gunfire, and it was a warning to this patrol of the European Monitoring Mission. I learned about this incident later on and requested that an investigation be undertaken. I was sent a written report from the assistant for security. He told me that the perpetrators were the members of the Vitezovi, and the names were Josip, Goran Medjugorac, and Slaven Kraljevic. I called the commander of the Vitezovi, Mr. Darko Kraljevic, and asked that disciplinary measures be taken against the perpetrators, and I also asked him to inform me of what disciplinary measures had been taken. I also informed, in writing, the chief of the main staff of the HVO of this incident that had occurred, and I know that the assistant for security also sent his own report towards the office for security. I did not receive --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What did Mr. Kraljevic say, because I think I remember that he said he was independent from you. Then you're saying, "I called the commander of the Vitezovi, Mr. Kraljevic." What is his answer? "I'm independent and have nothing to do with you," or does he say, "Yes, I will lead the investigation and I will take the necessary disciplinary measures"?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, I told him when I got the results, that they were his soldiers, and I gave him the names. I asked him to undertake disciplinary measures against those soldiers, and he told me that he would do so, but I did not receive from him any further information as to what measures he had taken, and I informed the main staff of the HVO about the whole incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Slaven Kraljevic, one of the perpetrators of the incident, is he any relation to Darko Kraljevic, the commander of the Vitezovi?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was his brother that had taken part in the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the days that followed, the 6th of October, 1993, the BH army completely took over the Zabrdze area and mountain and the slopes going up to a feature called Jelin Skok. They practically made it impossible for helicopters to fly in, and it placed this area and the airspace above it under its control. Once again, in the course of the 6th of October, I received information from the intelligence service that the BH army would continue to attack Vitez until they had taken it over, taken over the Vitez municipality. I gave, in the course of the 6th of October, written information and informed the chief of the main staff of the HVO of the problem of the relationships between the head of the security centre and the assistant for security, and I asked him in writing, the chief of the main staff, to look into the problem and solve it as soon as possible. I asked that this should be done by the 8th of October, 1993. Next, I asked the operative section to prepare summarily all the requests that I had made in the course of September and sent to the military police so as for me to be able to have an insight into how the tasks had been executed and the requests made by the commander of the military police in September.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let us stop there for a moment and look to the military police. About the 4th of August, you appointed Marinko Palavra as commander. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber briefly how you undertook to reorganise the military police? What measures did you undertake? What steps did you take? Let us see outside this chronology how that evolved.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We had a difficulty in that respect because Marinko Palavra was an individual who had not performed military police duties previously. He was the commander, the chief of a civilian police unit, so that I had to spend a considerable amount of time myself studying military police rules and regulations taken over from the previous army. I had to give Marinko Palavra instructions and I had to train him, so to speak, in activities of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what was he by profession and what functions had he performed before the war?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honours, he was a professor, a PT professor, gymnastics, physical training, and he was the national representative of Bosnia-Herzegovina, he was a judo expert, and he was the director of a primary school as well, the principal of a primary school, I think in the Travnik municipality, which means that he had actually not much to do with the army except for having served his regular military service as a soldier, as indeed every other soldier had done. So that I informed him and tried to capacitate him for the post of commander of a battalion. I gave him the information that I had at my disposal, and I gave him some time to let him take stock of the situation and to give me his own proposals as to how the military police should be reorganised, how he saw this reorganisation, and then we went step by steps towards the formation of a command for the battalion and for selecting commanders for companies and for establishing military police units generally, and we endeavoured in this process to include into the military police honest young men who were, for the most part, at the front line. So one of the decisive criteria was that they should be honest young men and that they had had no criminal record previously in the civilian police files.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, General, what happened to the military policemen who were the perpetrators of violence and who had criminal records, the ones you inherited, so to speak, from the previous period?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There too we took step by step, and gradually we distanced from the military police the military policemen who had had criminal records. We removed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In what way did you select the cadres for the military police? How did you arrive at information as to who would be well-suited to the job?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, usually this was something that Mr. Palavra undertook as well as his associates, and they asked the commanders of part of the battlefront and the commanders of the villages or the commanders of a sector would ask for recommendations to tell them which of the soldiers from the front line would be well-suited to become a member of the military police. After this preliminary list was compiled of possibles, Palavra, with his associates, looked into the criminal records, whether they existed in police stations in Vitez, Busovaca, Novi Travnik, and in part in Travnik itself, particularly the section where the police station functioned, and it was in operation in Nova Bila. After all these checks had been made, we selected soldiers for the military police regardless of the fact that individuals had never, in fact, done any military police work before, either in the former Yugolav People's Army or anywhere, and then I would undertake to prepare these men. I would organise training for individual activities and tasks that military police do. I would do this together with the commanders of the battalions and the commanders of the companies from the military police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, excuse me for interrupting. General Blaskic, did you play a role in the selection or the appointment of Marinko Palavra as commander of the military police?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I did have a role in this in that I nominated him and I received approval from the chief of the main staff to do so; in other words, I nominated him, I proposed him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But I don't think you chose him only for his quality as a gymnastics teacher. Did you have any other reason? Was he a member of the HVO? Did he play a political role? Do you understand my question? You had so many troubles with the military police that I would think that you thought a lot before choosing a military police commander.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, he had no political duties, but I chose him. I studied his file well; I even visited him twice. At that time, he was unaware of the fact that he was one of the candidates. My personnel officer also endeavoured to find all the information available in the field. For me, the basic criteria were honesty, his professionalism in respect of the duties, and his sincerity and his work habits. He was an athlete, he used to be an athlete, and he worked in an elementary school, in fact, he was principal of an elementary school, so he had some -- he was an educator, but his decency was the basic criterion. He hadn't even been in the military police before or a soldier before the war in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: (No translation)

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. We're not getting an English translation. I interrupt so we could start from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I will repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In other words, after you had selected Palavra for the military police commander, from today's point of view, between 8 August and January 1994, how do you view his relation to you? I'm not trying to suggest. But in military terms, how would you evaluate him?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honours, regarding his relationship to me, he was professional and he was -- he was very professional in terms of the duties and in terms of the relationship of the superior and subordinate. I would just like to point out the environment in which he worked. He was forced to work as the military police commander and carry out tasks on the one hand and, on the other hand, he was also in a position to have to build up this organisation; in other words, the duties of the military police were there, were present, they existed, regardless of the level of organisation of this organisation, and I believe and my assessment is that he did the most he could in terms of both the organisation, establishment of the military police, and its work. He definitely enabled the chain of command to function more efficiently, and he gave a contribution to the overall defence, and I think it was thanks in part to his work that we were able to sustain the defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What happened next?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the course of the 6th of October, I asked that the military police conduct an investigation in relation to the incident which occurred with the European Monitoring Mission representatives, and during the day, we had another incident, that is, the officials of the SIS department shot at Zoran Maric, who was the mayor of Busovaca, and I again asked for an investigation to be carried out in relation to that incident, and I learned that the incident was caused by members of the SIS, S-I-S, centre, and that potentially a new unit had been established. I, at that time, had no information that a new unit had been formed. I later learned that this unit had been established, that it was called Alpha, and that it numbered 25 to 30 members. This unit, as well as the SIS centre itself, was completely independent of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone command. I also asked the civilian police in Vitez to assist me in identifying the members of this unit because I had no information on which basis they had been established and who was part of it. I also had a meeting with Palavra, the military police commander. We talked about personnel issues, about organisational issues, and about tasks and about training members of the military police for different tasks. This was on the 8th. On the 9th of October, in Novi Travnik, we had a tragic event when citizens from Novi Travnik went for a supply of water, a mother was carrying a child, two-and-a-half-year-old child, and while she was getting water in front of a cistern in Novi Travnik, a sniper killed the child and seriously wounded the mother. At 11.00, I had a meeting with members of the European Monitoring Mission. I have no names of the officials in my notes, but they notified me that they had problems in cooperating with the Ban Josip Jelacic Brigade personnel in Kiseljak. I explained to the officials of the European Monitoring Mission that I too had difficulties in communicating with Kiseljak and that I would try to take steps and work on re-establishing communication between Kiseljak and the Mission. On the 10th of October, I had a meeting with Mr. de la Mota and Colonel Duncan, commander of the British battalion. In this meeting, we discussed a number of issues, and I'm going to list them here. The first issue was the evacuation of the wounded from Stari Vitez and the church hospital. In Stari Vitez, the wounded were members of the BH army, and in the church hospital, the wounded were members of the HVO. Second, the issue of fuel for the generator in the Nova Bila hospital which I had asked the UNHCR or UNPROFOR, I asked for assistance in delivery of that fuel, and also the issue of food for some 30.000 displaced persons and refugees in the Lasva area. I said that we had 75.000 people crowded in a very small area, and I also asked for information about the detained Croats in Zenica. I also pointed out the problems with the water supplies, and I told the representatives of the UNPROFOR and UNHCR that Vitez was without water, that Novi Travnik was without water, and that the hospital was without water and that the water pumps were all under the control of the BH army. I also asked that the water supply be reinstated. Also discussed was the issue of the separated families, in other words, Croats who happened to be in Vitez and their families were in Zenica and also some Bosniak Muslims who were in Zenica and their families had been left behind in Vitez. This was also an opportunity for me to address the issues of the difference in positions of the UNHCR and UNPROFOR because representatives of both sides were there. I asked them if they would harmonise their positions and I would help them subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that you were trying to reunite families if one member of the family was in Zenica and wanted to reunite with the rest of the family in Vitez, say. What was the position of the UNHCR?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The position of the UNHCR was that any movements of the families, any settlement of the families amounted to ethnic cleansing, and the positions that I had and the Red Cross had, the UNHCR had, was that we wanted them reunited. So we had a difference in positions, and I said that if those positions were harmonised, that I would support that unified position. The conclusions of the meeting were that the fuel for the hospital and for the fire fighting unit would be provided, that the UNHCR would assist in providing food for the displaced persons and refugees, that they would mediate in trying to reopen the supplies of water in Novi Travnik and in the church hospital, and that they will work on acquiring information about the detained Croats. As far as the reunification of families was concerned, the UNHCR representative, de la Mota, said that in individual but exceptional cases, after a verification process by the UNHCR, they would reunite individual families. On the 11th of October, 1993, we had a renewed attack at all defence lines by the BH army in Vitez, and again at 14.00, I called a meeting with all sector commanders in order to counter this attack and reinforce the defence. The attack was coming from the south side, from the direction of Zabrdze and the explosives factory. On 13 October, 1993, I received information from the chief of the Military Intelligence Service that the BH army was bringing in forces from Sarajevo and Tuzla in the BH army 3rd Corps zone of responsibility and that most probably these forces would be used for the conquest of Vitez and Busovaca. In the course of the day of the 13th of October, I learned about a new phenomenon which was the self-wounding of soldiers at the line of defence. It had become a frequent kind of incident, that the soldiers would wound themselves and then be transferred to the hospital where they would receive medical treatment and would be taken away from the front line. Again, there were rumours about the selling out of the territory, that is, the exchange of territory of Central Bosnia for the Mostar area, and they had a debilitating effect on the morale at the front line. Again, on the 13th of October, I asked the military police commander to allow the passage of a UNHCR convoy. This was a convoy carrying food to Stari Vitez. Again, this convoy was blocked by civilians, mostly women from Vitez, because they were suspicious of the convoy carrying ammunition and demanded that the convoy be checked. I issued an order to the military police to convince the civilians to let the convoy pass, and after some convincing, the humanitarian aid passed through to Stari Vitez. I also asked for the military police to conduct an investigation relating to the stolen vehicles, UNHCR vehicles, and the investigation later produced some results. We managed to have three UNHCR vehicles returned. They were discovered with members of the Vitezovi, and they already had been properly registered with the civilian police authorities in Vitez. In the course of the day, logistic support was parachuted by helicopter from Mostar, and I was informed that a Vitezovi unit had received 10.600 pieces of ammunition. This was a surprise for me because they had asked for 7.000. Usually, we would get less than we asked for. In this case, the opposite was true. The commander had requested less, yet he received more ammunition than he had asked for, even though it was in such short supply for us. The helicopters, once the BH army had taken control of Zabrdze, landed very rarely, and they would mostly drop ammunition and other materiel by parachute, as the only way of providing logistics support to the Lasva pocket. At 18.00, I had another meeting with Commander Palavra, and together, we studied the rules on the work of the crime department of the military police, trying to organise ourselves and organise the work of the crime department and to select new personnel because we had learnt that the members of that service were collaborating with local criminal gangs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: General, Palavra had taken over command of the 4th Military Police Battalion, and you were Palavra's superior. Did Palavra have control over the entire military police in Central Bosnia or did a part of the military police remain outside his command, which means outside yours as well?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: A part of the military police still remained outside my authority and his, which means that Palavra did not have control over any other military police unit, except of the 4th Battalion, which was later called the 7th Battalion. There was a light assault battalion of the military police which was not under Palavra's control, nor did I have any control over that unit in control and command terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, General. When the military police was attached to you, which you wanted for a long time, were you told that you would not have command over the whole military police?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. A battalion of the military police was attached to me. It was directly under my command in terms of control and command, but there was another military police unit which, in the period I'm referring to now, was not directly subordinated to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Now, let us explain with a few questions the nature of that unit. Tell us, what was the difference between the light assault battalion, which was not subordinated to you or Marinko Palavra, and the 7th or 4th Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The military police battalion was mainly intended for military police work, whereas the light assault battalion was a combat unit of the military police designed for combat operations carried out by military police forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: That light assault military police battalion, which, as you said, was designed exclusively for combat purposes, what was its name on the 16th of April, 1993? What were its origins?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was called the anti-terrorist platoon of the military police, and they referred to themselves as the Jokers, but this anti-terrorist platoon was increased to the level of a battalion which came to be called the light assault battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: If you were not in command of that light assault battalion, formally the Jokers, and if Marinko Palavra, your subordinate, was not in command of it, who was in command of that unit?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That unit was directly subordinate to the chief of the military police department in Mostar, and for a short time, and when I say "short," I mean a period of one month roughly, that unit was under the command of the chief of the military police administration through the assistant chief in each Operative Zone, which means that throughout the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, there were four Operative Zones, and each Operative Zones had one assistant chief of the military police department. That chief of the military police administration was in command of those units through his assistants in those zones.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who was it in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: For a time, it was Mr. Pasko Ljubicic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Can we therefore understand that this unit, the Jokeri, could intervene following point 8 of article 10 of the rules that were used by the Defence yesterday and which relates to the activities of the military police? Do you remember I asked some questions about this point, point 8? It was struggling against terrorism, rebellion, and other enemy groups; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Can we therefore interpret what you say as the following: The Jokeri, this assault unit, could have taken part in the events at Ahmici following point 8 of article 10 of these rules?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In accordance with point 8 -- as far as I remember, that one referred to struggle against sabotage groups -- it could intervene. It is rather ambiguous, as I myself said, because for that particular point, no special permission from the defence minister was required.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Nobilo, that we will wait for some clarifications on this problem of rules and regulations. Because today we're talking about the Jokeri, the anti-terrorist group, the 7th Battalion, which was also entitled to take part in the events, and I think we will need some clarification on that point in due time. We can now take the break, a 20-minute break. We will start again at twenty to twelve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Please be seated. Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: General, I think we had stopped when discussing the 14th of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. On the 14th of October, 1993, offensive operations and fighting continued, and in the second half of the night between the 14th and the 15th, UNPROFOR members brought three members of the HVO in front of the Vitez Hotel, the command building, who had been caught stealing fuel from the United Nations logistics base in Nova Bila. They were handed over to the officer on duty. These were members of the Vitez Brigade. The following day, I wrote a letter of thanks to the UNPROFOR commander for cooperating with us in preventing crime, and I issued 60 days of military detention as a disciplinary measure for all three.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was that the maximum penalty you could give?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. At the press conference, I condemned this act of crime, and I publicly expressed my gratitude for all assistance given in crime prevention, and I also appealed to others to assist and support us in preventing crime in the area of the Lasva pocket. I also had a meeting with members of the command in the course of the day, and we discussed the question of crime and robberies and also the usurpation of apartments, mostly belonging to Bosniak Muslims, in Vitez, Novi Travnik, and partly in Busovaca as well. In the afternoon, I had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, General. When you said you examined or discussed the problem of the occupation of apartments, what does that actually mean? Because you took a number of orders regarding evictions, confiscation of homes; these were Exhibits 316 and so on, I think. But at a meeting of this kind, on the 14th of October, you kept repeating that apartments should not be appropriated by people who had left or did you take sanctions? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, when examining such incidents regarding the usurpation of departments, I tried to discover who was behind it, whether it was displaced persons who were very numerous - there were about 35.000 of them in the small areas - or was it done by soldiers or members of the military police, the former military police, which were most prominent in such incidents? If the soldiers were behind it, then I would give orders to the military police to throw out the usurpers and to restore the apartments to the proper owners. I even gave orders for guard duty to be organised in front of these dwellings so that the owners would feel safer, and there were such cases too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But you already had issued such orders, General Blaskic, at least a month or two months previously. Did you keep repeating orders? Did you have real sanctions? What did you actually undertake? I don't doubt that this must have been a major problem, to have 35.000 refugees around you, and you had to take care of all of that in addition to waging war, but when you did address the issue, what exactly did you do, because you had already issued orders at least a month or two months previously on expulsions and the question of dwellings.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: When I received a list with the names of the perpetrators, I issued orders to the military police to throw out soldiers from apartments regardless of whether they were displaced persons or not. If a soldier was in an apartment that had been owned by a Bosniak Muslim, he would be thrown out and the original owners would be restored, if that was possible. That was the concrete step I took. I even had talks with individual Bosniak Muslim families and told them to go back to their apartments, and their answer would be, "What's the point of going back if we're going to be evicted again in two days' time?" Then I said, "Very well. You will have guards in front of your apartments so that you can be sure that you will not be evicted again." So there were even such very specific measures taken by me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, do you have evidence of this? Do you have documents confirming these specific actions taken?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We have the orders whereby General Blaskic prohibited such things, then we have another order naming the military policemen who had entered other people's apartments and for whom disciplinary measures were requested, and we have the testimony of General Blaskic who remembers specific cases when he provided protection to individual families. For when he sent a patrol to throw out a soldier and bring back the Muslim family, there is nothing in writing, no written trace about this, there is no written order for such a concrete, specific case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nobilo. General Blaskic, in this area of the occupation of flats and houses by others, did you have any cooperation with others or any manner of contacting the civilian authorities, or was this a problem that you alone had to deal with?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me say first that Vitez for me was an unknown entity too because I hadn't spent a minute in that town before the war, so I asked the mayor to provide me with a list of dwellings that he knew or his bodies knew that their owners had been evicted from, and only when I received that list -- I myself was surprised, I think there were about 39 flats or a total of 53 dwellings that had been seized by the military police, and I had expected that same military to punish such tendencies. So this happened before. After that, the mayor and I tried to thwart such attempts and to prevent them, so we did coordinate, we would coordinate on the phone, and at one point we organised a meeting for the people behind the evictions and those whose responsibility it was to punish such evictions. So I did cooperate with the mayor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Continue, Mr. Nobilo, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: General, let us continue with the chronology of events.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 14th of October, in the evening, I was informed that a helicopter was about to arrive for the transportation of the wounded, and I called Mr. Palavra for us to deal with the problem of security to make sure that only the heavily wounded should be boarded on the helicopter because we feared that the refugees would crowd together and try to occupy the places intended for the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, General, in your assessment, you just said that the refugees wanted to get on the helicopter and get away. In your assessment, if the BH army had allowed free passage, a free corridor, between Vitez and Busovaca and Herzegovina and said, "Through the international organisation, we guarantee safety to all passing through that corridor," what would have happened?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Under conditions of absolute hunger and a shortage of everything but death, I do believe that everyone would have left the area. Let me just add, many moral values were reversed. All the burials took place at night, not one during the daytime. I remember that I was surprised when I noticed unusual behaviour among my associates on one occasion and I asked what was happening, and then they told me from the operations department, "Nobody was killed today." And that was strange; it was an unusual day. Everybody was surprised that nobody had been killed. Unfortunately, there were very few such days.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: As an example, a package with twenty cigarettes, how much was it worth in this pocket where you were?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The lowest price was 70 and it went up to 100 German marks, and one handmade cigarette made with tobacco would be shared between three to five soldiers, if any were available. I have an example at the end of the month when the assistant for logistics asked me how to deal with a problem of one kilogram of powder milk and how to share it among 52 children.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What was your diet in those days?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: All the soldiers on the front line received at 10.00 a.m. lentils or rice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was there any meat?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. In the afternoon, they mostly ate rice. So it was either lentils or rice. Towards the end of November, there was no bread even to distribute to the soldiers, so actually, they only had two meals mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Go on, please.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 15th of October, 1993, at about 18.30, the commander of the military police informed me that at the Bobasi front line, a military policeman called Zeba had spoken to his colleague from the 17th Krajina Brigade of the BH army, and they knew each other because they were both in the Kotor Varos battalion before, that is, from the days of 1992, and his friend, who was in this case the attacker, said to Zeba, and I quote: "There can be no agreement with the HVO. We have been ordered to go until the end. The 7th Muslim Brigade will attack from the north and kill the Croats once it enters Vitez."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what was the belief of the 70.000 Croats which had been pushed into the pocket of the Lasva River Valley? What did they think would happen to them if your defence fell? What was the general belief, conviction?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, there was the belief that it would be total destruction, that most of them would be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 17th of October, 1993, the commander of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade asked me to temporarily halt all disciplinary measures being carried out in the military detention centre, and he said that the disciplinary measures had, in fact, become stimulative measures, that is to say, in his own brigade in Novi Travnik, the soldiers intentionally carried out offences so as to receive disciplinary measures and be sent to detention centres and thus avoid going to the front line, so that there were many more breaches than was usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, General, in the morning, your soldiers had lentils to eat, they had rice in the afternoon, sometimes with bread, sometimes without bread. What was the situation like in the Kaonik prison camp?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, according to my knowledge and the information that I received, in the Kaonik prison camp, the detainees were given three meals a day. They did not have three meals a day even in the hospital. The wounded people were sometimes given two meals a day. Sometimes we would have vegetable fat, and we would give it out for breakfast.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In Busovaca, on the 17th of October, an attack was launched on the parish office in Busovaca and the Caritas warehouse. This was done by uniformed individuals. Foodstuffs were taken for the most part, rice and oil. Also in the course of the 17th of October, there was an artillery attack in the centre of the town of Vitez and a trial had been organised in the District Court of Vitez when these activities were under way. At 10.00, I got a call from the mayor, Ivica Santic, and he asked me whether we were going to be able to hold out, what were my assessments, and would we be able to hold out in our defence? Sometime between 11.00 and 12.00 on that day, I had a meeting with Colonel Duncan, the commander of the BritBat, and he informed me that a meeting would be held in Kiseljak and that the meeting would be attended by General Petkovic who was, at the time, the deputy chief of the main staff of the HVO. I told Colonel Duncan that I was very worried with the situation in the Lasva pocket and the food shortage there, and he told me, Colonel Duncan told me, that is, that he was surprised that the HVO had not organised a convoy for Central Bosnia from the Republic of Croatia or perhaps from Herzegovina, and I told him on the occasion, I said, "What road should we use?" because communications were not under our control.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, please, General, if you can remember, when was the last time a convoy reached the area of Central Bosnia from Herzegovina with foodstuffs? When was the last one?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember the exact date, it is difficult to say, but it was -- there were no convoys from, say, April 1993. I'm sure that not a single convoy arrived. The only food that was distributed was the food that we were able to come by from the UNHCR, and that food was given to the refugees as a priority. So the UNHCR fed the refugees. That was its task.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I also discussed with Colonel Duncan matters of communication, the situation at the front line, and I told him that, in fact, I was most preoccupied with survival in the region; and on the 17th, in the course of the day, I received information that the commander of the special purposes unit, Darko Kraljevic, for the needs of foreign television crews, had carried out some faked operations, placing explosives in our trenches and the activation of the same and then opened fire while this was being filmed by the foreign television crews, and I think I even saw a clip from that material that was taped. I think that it was even shown here. But this was, as I say, staged for the filming activities. There were no combat results in the operations that were undertaken by him on that occasion. I received written information about this from the assistant for security, and I myself informed the chief of the main staff of the HVO of those developments. On the 18th of October, 1993, the attack continued on Vitez and Travnik, and that same day in Busovaca, throughout the day, it was peaceful, quiet, but around 17.00, a projectile fell, artillery projectiles fell in the centre of the town of Busovaca, and eight civilians were seriously injured. I also received information that up until the 18th of October, from the 3rd of September, there were four helicopter flights bringing in about eight tonnes of cargo, materiel, and technical equipment. In the course of the 18th of October, I had a meeting with the IPD, the assistant for Information and Propaganda Activities, and we looked at the situation and the fatigue that was being caused, neuroses, rumours, the sensitivity of the soldiers themselves, and the general drop of overall morale. Morale was very low, particularly at the front line with the soldiers there. We discussed how to tackle this question and solve it and improve morale with the fighters, with the people. I also received information from the main staff in the course of the 18th of October telling me that the pilots of the Croatian Defence Council did not wish and could no longer fly because of fatigue and because of constant combat operations so that they had decided to halt supplies to Vitez from the 18th of October onwards. On the 19th of October, activities continued. In the early morning, there were artillery attacks on part of the Busovaca battlefront at the Kaonik feature, the crossroads of the Vitez-Busovaca-Zenica road. On that day, a convoy passed by for the purposes of the BH army. The convoy was running towards Novi Travnik, Travnik, Guca Gora, and across Stranjani and Cajdras to Zenica. The convoy passed by without impediment from the HVO --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: It was the convoy of the BH army, was it not?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it was a BH army convoy which passed by in the direct vicinity of the front line, but the entire road at that time was controlled by the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: If you let their convoy pass by, do you not think that the main staff of the HVO in Mostar could have organised a convoy which would take assistance to you? How do you view that issue?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I can only assume that an agreement of that kind could have been reached because this convoy could have been stopped by the units in the Lasva pocket, but we did not hamper the free passage of the convoy, and the convoy did go through without any HVO attacks and it entered Zenica. Quite possibly there could have been an agreement to send a joint convoy, all the more so as in December 1993, joint convoys were sent. So if this was possible in December 1993, then it could have been possible in October 1993 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The food that was loaded up in the convoys, how did it enter Bosnia-Herzegovina, according to your knowledge, and how was it taken to Zenica? Via which territory? Which territory did it have to pass through?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, all the food had to pass from the Republic of Croatia via the area controlled by the HVO and further on towards the areas controlled by the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 19th of October at 15.00, I had a telephone conversation with the defence minister, Bruno Stojic, and he told me that he would mediate in the transport of weapons which the municipal officials of the municipalities of Busovaca, Vitez, Novi Travnik, and Travnik, the authorities there had decided to purchase on the market for the soldiers of the HVO, and he asked me to cooperate with the presidents of the municipalities and to send in specifications as to what kind of weapons we needed, the weapons most necessary for defence in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you get the weapons?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, we got the weapons after the signing of the Washington Agreement. It arrived into the Lasva River Valley, but it did not arrive before that; and, as I say, the weapons were bought on the market.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 19th of October, in the second half of the day, I sent the defence minister a written proposal for changing the organisation in the Lasva pocket, and the essence of my proposal was to disband the special purpose units and to form a unit which would be created as a unit directly subordinate to me. I gave the example that it could be called a guard unit, that was my proposal, and I included the disbanding of the Vitezovi, the Tvrtko unit, and the light assault battalion. That proposal was sent on the 19th of October, 1993. On the 20th of October, 1993, we once again looked into the problems of disciplinary measures and the lack of manpower up at the front line and a situation in which these disciplinary measures were a stimulative measure. On the 21st of October, 1993, I asked that, in the town of Vitez, signs be put up which would caution citizens where sniper fire was coming from and that in the streets large banners should be set up and canvasses so as make it impossible for snipers from Stari Vitez to fire on the citizens of Vitez, to block their view, in fact. This was one of the ways of protecting the population from losing their lives from sniper fire. So the operations continued. I also received information on the 21st of October that in the Lasva pocket, about 80 children were left either without one or both parents who had been killed during the combat operations. On that day, we received assistance from the UNHCR. The UNHCR brought in four truckloads of foodstuffs for Kruscica and four truckloads for the Vitez municipality which was under the control of the civilian authorities. We again had the problem that the civilians hindered the passage of the convoy to Kruscica, again demanding control and again expressing their suspicion that it was ammunition which was being transported. Also on the 21st of October, the assistance reached the church hospital in Nova Bila. I issued an order during that day that all long-barrelled weapons be sent to the front line and that these types of weapons not be used away from the front lines. This was sent to all the HVO units. I also received information from Novi Travnik that the Serbs were trying to leave the area of Novi Travnik. I was informed of this by the commander of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade in Novi Travnik, and I said to him that he should convey our position to the civilian authorities of Novi Travnik. Our position was that, in principle, we were against their leaving the area and that we were supporting the UNHCR position that everybody should remain in their own homes. I do not know exactly how this case, that is, this request of the Serbian citizens of Novi Travnik ended. I believe that a part of them left and that another part remained in Novi Travnik. They had left Novi Travnik via Travnik under the auspices of the international organisations. On the 22nd of October, I received information from the communications officer, Mr. Gelic, that the BH army in Zeljezno Polje had executed mobilised Croatian recruits who had been mobilised in Zenica for having refused to fight Croats in Zepce. I later asked that this information be confirmed, I asked it of Colonel Duncan, and this information was not confirmed. At 13.35, in Travnik, there was a duel between the local criminal gang leaders, Tuka on the one side and Zuti on the other side. It was a classic gun battle in which Tuka had seriously wounded Zuti. Later on, two brigades from that area, the Frankopan Brigade and the Travnik Brigade, had a confrontation, and it was really the sympathisers of the two gang lords who confronted each other. I tried to calm down the situation among the Travnik brigades. I said that this was not a way to resolve things, and I issued an order to the military police and the security office to conduct an investigation. The next day, on the 23rd of October, there was a renewed confrontation, and the tensions were rising between the Frankopan and the Travnik Brigade. On the 24th of October, the military police commander had punished two military policemen for their improper carrying out of given orders, and they were sent to the detention unit. This was big news because, up until then, very few disciplinary measures had been given to the soldiers. I also had a meeting with Miso Mijic, the chief of the SIS office, and he said that the SIS centre would undertake --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Let's further specify the record. You said that it was very rare that people went to the military prison. Was it the soldiers or the military policemen?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The military policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The record says that disciplinary measures had been given to soldiers, whereas you said that it was very rarely given to the military policemen?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, before that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Why don't you just repeat your answer regarding the disciplinary measures?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The military police commander punished two military policemen and sentenced them to the military detention for their failure to perform their military police duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And then what was your comment to this?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that this was an event, it was news, because it had been rare until then that the military policemen were sent to detention for their failure to perform or carry out their duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. We have cleared up the transcript. Let's move on to the meeting with Miso Mijic of the SIS centre, and if you can just shed some light on the problems with the SIS centre in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The SIS centre still worked independently, on its own. Miso Mic, the chief of the SIS centre, told me that he intended to take over complete control of the explosives factory, as well as all the helicopter flights and helicopter transports. From this, I concluded that there had been no response to my request that this problem of the SIS centre and its role be resolved by the competent security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: General, please remind us, who was the deputy chief of the SIS centre?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The deputy chief of the SIS centre was the commander of the Vitezovi, Darko Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In your opinion, why did Darko Kraljevic and Miso Mijic from the SIS centre want to take control of the explosives factory and of the helicopter flights and drops?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In this way, they would be able not only to control their own logistics supplies, which they were receiving directly from the main staff, but also the logistics supplies of the Operative Zone and, in that way, control the manner in which the defence was being conducted and also, in that way, they would have at their disposal the valuable technology, administration, and everything else that had to do with the explosives factory, including its role in the defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Nobilo, that will be enough for today. I should like us to stop there. We need another five minutes in closed session to discuss our programme for the first week of April. We won't need more than five or six minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President. We can stop there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let's have a private session then, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 1.42 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 6th day of April, 1999, at10.00 a.m. 24
